To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the medial prefronto-limbic-striatal system and the default network of brain areas, which have been implicated in normal emotional behavior, are altered in depression.

1) the MPFC and closely related structures in the medial and orbital cortex, amygdala, and basal ganglia show alterations in grey matter and functional activity in cases with recurrent major depression; 2) these areas are part of a larger network of structures that includes the dorsal PFC that has been implicated in the regulation of self-referential processes; 3) the MPFC is also part of the forebrain limbic system that modulates autonomic and neuroendocrine functions

structural and functional abnormalities of brain regions that are part of the default system are associated with the pathophysiology, and that the default system is a key component of a neural network that regulates emotional behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiological basis of mood disorders, and in particular the neural circuits that underlie emotional behavior and the neurochemical systems and their receptors that regulate these circuits.
elucidating the structural and functional neuroanatomical correlates of depression and related affective disorders.
the neural networks that putative modulate aspects of emotional behavior and how these networks are altered in mood disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

mood disorders involve dysfunction in the MPFC and its related limbic and subcortical structures, and that this dysfunction can be conceptualized within a framework that incorporates the neurocircuits involved in normal emotional behavior.
there is no single brain region that is responsible for depression.

the neurocircuits implicated in mood disorders involve a distributed set of brain structures, including the MPFC and its closely related limbic and paralimbic structures, which are modulated by a variety of neurochemical systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mood disorders are associated with structural and functional abnormalities of neural systems that are involved in the modulation of normal emotional behavior.
the MPFC network and related structures form the neurocircuitry basis of depression and that their dysfunction is the neurobiological substrate for depressive syndromes.
the MPFC network is a key component of the neurocirculatory that modulates emotional behavior and is a critical component of the neural circuitry that underlies mood disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MPFC network, which is involved in the processing of emotional information, is a key player in the pathogenesis of mood disorders.
the MPFC is the key structure that integrates emotional, cognitive, autonomic, and neuroendocrine aspects of mood disorders.
the MPFC, amygdala, and related limbic, striatal and cortical structures form a neurocircuitry that modulates emotional expression and other aspects of mood regulation.
